label: Book of Giants (Sefer HaNephilim) — Complete — Fragments 1–6
summary_plain: The Book of Giants tells the story of the Nephilim — the offspring of the Watchers and human women. The giants Ohya and Hahya receive terrifying dreams warning of the coming flood. They send Mahaway to Chanokh to interpret the dreams. Chanokh confirms: the destruction is coming because of what the Watchers did. Gilgamesh is named as one of the Nephilim. The text survives in Aramaic fragments from Qumran — 4Q203, 4Q530, 4Q531, 4Q532.
summary_scholarly: The Book of Giants is preserved in Aramaic fragments from Qumran Cave 4 (4Q203, 4Q530-532). It is absent from the Ge'ez Orit — the text was not transmitted to Africa through the Greek translation chain. The fragments name Gilgamesh — the central figure of Mesopotamian mythology — as a Nephilim, directly connecting the Sumerian dynastic tradition to the Watcher/Nephilim framework. The giants Ohya and Hahya receive dream visions of the coming flood. They send the messenger Mahaway flying to Chanokh at the ends of the earth to interpret the dreams. Chanokh delivers the judgment: the tablet of destruction has been issued. The text fills the gap between the Watcher descent in Chanokh 6-16 and the flood narrative in Bereshit 6-9.

key_terms.definition: The offspring of the Watchers and the daughters of men — giants of enormous size and strength who filled the earth with violence before the flood. 1 Chanokh and the Book of Giants describe their deeds and judgment. Their spirits remain as evil spirits after death.

The heavenly beings (irin) who descended to earth and took human wives, transgressing their station. The Book of Giants is focused on their offspring — the Nephilim — and the chaos the giants created.
One of the giant sons of the Watcher Shemihaza in the Book of Giants. He and his brother Hahya are central figures. Ohya has ominous dreams and debates their meaning with the other giants.
The brother of Ohya — a giant son of Shemihaza. Together Ohya and Hahya are terrified by their dreams of cosmic destruction and seek out Mahway to carry a message to Chanokh.
A giant, son of the Watcher Barakel, who travels through the air to find Chanokh and ask him to interpret the giants' terrifying dreams. Mahway functions as the giants' messenger and petitioner.

The heavenly tablets that Chanokh possesses and that the giants in the Book of Giants are desperate to have read. The tablets contain the judgment decreed against the Nephilim and the Watchers — YHWH's verdict that the giants will be destroyed.

Warriors / mighty ones — a term used for the Nephilim alongside 'Nephilim.' Bereshit 6:4 calls them 'the mighty men who were of old, men of renown.' The Book of Giants portrays them as violent destroyers of both humans and animals.

The central narrative event of the Book of Giants: Ohya and Hahya have terrifying dreams of a great garden being destroyed and a figure with water tablets washing away everything. These dreams presage the coming flood judgment. The giants cannot interpret the dreams themselves and send Mahway to find Chanokh.

The leader of the Watchers who descended — the chief of the two hundred who swore the oath together on Mount Hermon to take human wives. His sons Ohya and Hahya are prominent in the Book of Giants. 1 Chanokh 6-7 names him first among the Watcher leaders.

The primary Aramaic fragments of the Book of Giants found in Cave 4 at Qumran. Combined with 4Q203, 1Q23, 2Q26, and 6Q8, they give a partial but coherent text. The Manichaean Book of Giants, adapted from the Enochic tradition, provides additional comparative evidence for the original narrative.

faq.question: What is the Book of Giants?
faq.answer: The Book of Giants is an Aramaic text from the Enochic tradition, found in fragments at Qumran (4Q203, 4Q530-4Q533, 1Q23, 2Q26, 6Q8). It expands on the Watcher narrative of 1 Chanokh, focusing on the Nephilim giants — specifically the sons of Shemihaza, Ohya and Hahya — and their ominous dreams presaging the coming flood judgment. The giants send Mahway to find Chanokh and ask for dream interpretation. Chanokh's response, carried back by Mahway, confirms the judgment: the Nephilim will be destroyed. No Aramaic complete copy survived — the text is reconstructed from multiple fragmentary manuscripts.

faq.question: How does the Book of Giants relate to 1 Chanokh?
faq.answer: The Book of Giants is part of the same Enochic tradition as 1 Chanokh and elaborates the Watcher narrative from a different angle. While 1 Chanokh focuses on Chanokh himself — his journeys, visions, and the heavenly verdict — the Book of Giants focuses on the Nephilim's perspective: their fear, their dreams, their failed attempt to appeal through Chanokh. The two texts are complementary. The Qumran community treated both as authoritative, preserving multiple copies of each. The Book of Giants is older than the Manichaean version that adapted it, which helps confirm the Qumran text's priority.

faq.question: Who is Mahway and why is his role important?
faq.answer: Mahway is a giant son of the Watcher Barakel who travels through the air to reach Chanokh and present the giants' petition. His role is theologically significant: even the Nephilim, who are the product of the Watchers' transgression, seek YHWH's verdict through Chanokh — the righteous human who walked with YHWH. The giants cannot reverse their judgment, but the narrative shows them acknowledging the authority of the heavenly court. Mahway functions as the threshold figure between the condemned giants and the heavenly authority that condemned them.

faq.question: What do the giants' dreams signify?
faq.answer: In the Book of Giants, Ohya and Hahya have terrible dreams of a great garden being uprooted — trees falling, water tablets washing away names, and cosmic destruction. The dreams are YHWH's advance warning to the giants that their time is ending. The giants cannot interpret the dreams themselves — they lack the wisdom of Chanokh, who was taken up to receive heavenly knowledge. The dreams establish that even the most powerful physical beings are subject to YHWH's judgment and have no access to the heavenly wisdom that would let them understand it without a mediator.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of evil spirits coming from the Nephilim's bodies?
faq.answer: 1 Chanokh 15 explains that after the Nephilim die in the flood, their spirits do not go to Sheol like normal human spirits but remain on earth as evil spirits — orphaned, disembodied, corrupting and afflicting humanity. This provides the Enochic explanation for the ongoing presence of evil in the post-flood world: the original transgression of the Watchers left a residue. The flood destroyed the Nephilim's bodies but their spirits remain until the final judgment. This framework is foundational to the DSS community's understanding of the present era's spiritual warfare.

faq.question: What is the connection between the Book of Giants and Manichaean literature?
faq.answer: The Manichaean Book of Giants, written centuries after the Qumran text, adapted the Enochic narrative — but replaced some figures with Zoroastrian names and added Manichaean theological content. The existence of the Manichaean version confirms that the Enochic Book of Giants was widely known and influential in the ancient world. When comparing the two versions, the Qumran text's priority is clear: the Manichaean version borrowed from the Enochic tradition, not the reverse. This is another example of the ancient covenant texts being the source tradition — the later adaptation is derived from them.

faq.question: How does the Book of Giants treat the question of accountability?
faq.answer: The Book of Giants does not present the Nephilim as simply monsters — they are terrified, they seek information, they try to appeal their judgment. This creates a nuanced picture: the giants are accountable for the violence they caused, and that accountability is real and final. But they are also products of their fathers' transgression — they did not choose to be born Nephilim. The text does not resolve this tension; it presents the judgment as YHWH's just verdict and Chanokh's confirmation of it. The Qumran community found in this narrative a template for understanding their own era: the corrupt powers that dominated them were accountable, and YHWH's judgment would come.

faq.question: Why is the Book of Giants important for understanding the DSS community's worldview?
faq.answer: The Book of Giants, alongside 1 Chanokh, provided the Qumran community with their explanation of the present world's corruption. The Watchers' transgression introduced forbidden knowledge, violence, and spiritual contamination into the created order. The flood did not fully eliminate the problem — evil spirits remain. The community's strict purity rules, their separation from the corrupted mainstream, and their calendar observance were all responses to this framework. They were the remnant preserving covenant purity in a world still contaminated by the Watchers' legacy, waiting for YHWH's final judgment to complete what the flood began.

faq.question: What is the significance of Shemihaza as the Watcher leader?
faq.answer: Shemihaza (also spelled Semyaza or Shemyaza in various manuscripts) is named in 1 Chanokh 6:3 as the leader of the Watchers who swore the oath on Mount Hermon. His sons Ohya and Hahya are the most prominent Nephilim in the Book of Giants. By naming a specific leader responsible for organizing the transgression, 1 Chanokh and the Book of Giants assign moral responsibility to a named agent rather than treating the fall as anonymous or inevitable. The oath sworn by the two hundred Watchers — a collective choice — makes all of them accountable. The Book of Giants traces the consequences of that choice through the generations to the giants themselves.

faq.question: What does the Book of Giants reveal about ancient understanding of cosmic hierarchy?
faq.answer: The Book of Giants assumes a clear cosmic hierarchy: YHWH at the top, angels (Watchers) in the intermediate realm, humans on earth, animals below humans. The Watchers' transgression was crossing the boundary between their station (heavenly) and the human realm — taking wives and producing hybrid offspring. This boundary-crossing corrupted both realms: the heavenly beings became earthly, and earthly beings became gigantic violators of normal creaturely limits. The Nephilim are the living embodiment of a violated cosmic order. The judgment — the flood — is the restoration of proper boundaries. This framework underlies all the Enochic tradition's treatment of purity, separation, and covenant discipline.
